passages.t: ‘Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD’
passages.happening:
Psalm 95 has no heading. It is a call to worship. “Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD; let us shout to the Rock of our salvation” (verse 1). “Let us enter His presence with thanksgiving” (verse 2).

It gives the reason. “For the LORD is a great God, a great King above all gods” (verse 3). Everything belongs to him: the deep places of the earth, the mountain peaks, the sea and the dry land (verses 4 to 5). “The sea is His, for He made it, and His hands formed the dry land” (verse 5).

Then the call changes from shouting to kneeling. “O come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD our Maker” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Many scholars think this psalm was sung as worshippers came into the temple courts. It moves like a procession: first joyful noise, then entering, then bowing down.

The nations around Israel had gods for each part of the world: a god of the sea, a god of the storm, gods of the mountains, gods below the earth. Psalm 95 walks across that whole map, deep places, peaks, sea and land, and puts every part of it in the LORD's hand. To call him ‘a great King above all gods’ was a bold claim in that world.

Bowing and kneeling (verse 6) was how a subject came before a king. Worship used the same body language. It was not only words and songs. People bent their knees.

Psalm 95 is one of the psalms that sing that the LORD is King. Psalm 93 began the theme; 96 to 99 carry it on.
passages.later: Paul looks to a day when “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10). In Revelation, the elders around God's throne sing, “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things” (Revelation 4:11).
passages.asks:
How do you come into worship? Psalm 95 moves from loud joy to quiet kneeling. Both belong. If you only ever do one, try the other this week.

Notice the reason it gives for worship: God made everything, and he is King over all of it. Worship begins with seeing who he is.

passages.happening:
The psalm changes again. “For He is our God, and we are the people of His pasture, the sheep under His care” (verse 7). Then, suddenly, a warning: “Today, if you hear His voice” (verse 7), “do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness” (verse 8).

God himself speaks of the place “where your fathers tested and tried Me, though they had seen My work” (verse 9). “For forty years I was angry with that generation” (verse 10). “So I swore on oath in My anger, ‘They shall never enter My rest’” (verse 11).

That is how the psalm ends. A joyful song finishes with a warning.
passages.hearers:
Massah means ‘testing’ and Meribah means ‘quarrelling’. They were names for the place in the desert where the people, thirsty, demanded water and asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7). They had just seen God part the sea, and they still doubted him.

The ‘forty years’ are the years in the wilderness. After the people refused to enter the promised land, God said that the generation that had tested him would not see it (Numbers 14:22-23). Their ‘rest’ was the land itself, a home at last after slavery and wandering.

Why end a song of praise this way? Some scholars think a priest or prophet spoke God's warning after the people had sung. Others see it as the psalm's own design. Either way, the point is clear. Singing and bowing are empty if the heart stays closed.
passages.later:
Hebrews quotes these verses at length (Hebrews 3:7-11) and says they were spoken “through David” (Hebrews 4:7). It takes the word ‘Today’ seriously: “exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin's deceitfulness” (Hebrews 3:13).

Hebrews also says that the rest God promised was more than the land. “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). And Jesus said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
passages.asks:
‘Today’ is the key word. Not tomorrow, when you feel more ready. Today, if you hear God's voice in Scripture, in your conscience, in a friend's honest word, do not harden your heart.

Where have you seen God at work, and still asked, ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’ Psalm 95 is gentle and firm at once. It invites you to kneel, and warns you not to stay hard.
